chunks: Characterizing a differential pair's SI. The question: How do you characterize SI of a differential pair?
Checking a differential pair's signal quality means more than seeing that the eye looks open. You check it at three levels.
First the structure: right impedance, and two wires of equal length? Second the channel: how much signal is lost, and how much reflects?
Third the link: do real bits arrive correctly?
Think of a delivery route. First you inspect the road itself: is it the same width all the way, with no sudden bumps?
Then you measure what the trip does to the packages: how many get damaged or lost on the way? Last you run real deliveries and count how many arrive in good shape.
A measurement map. The first four boxes are properties of the channel you can measure without a live data stream; the last is the result with data running.
When the eye is bad, work backwards through the other four to find which property is responsible.
Differential impedance: the ratio of voltage to current that a signal traveling along the pair sees, set by the wires' size and spacing; often 100 ohms ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Intra-pair skew: a difference in arrival time between the pair's two wires. Insertion loss: how much the channel weakens the signal, in dB.
A 10 decibels loss leaves about 32% of the voltage. Mode conversion: part of the differential signal turning into common-mode (shared) signal because the pair is not symmetric.
Eye diagram: many bits overlaid on one picture, showing the timing and voltage room at the receiver ("What an eye diagram shows").
A pair is designed for 100 ohms. A test that measures impedance along the pair's length should show no bumps, for example at a via.
At 10 Gb/s one bit lasts 100 picoseconds, so 10 picoseconds of skew between the two wires is 10% of a bit. For the channel, say the loss is 10 decibels.
A 400 millivolts swing then arrives as about 0. 316 times 400 millivolts = 126 millivolts.
Last, the eye diagram at the receiver shows whether that weakened, skewed signal is still readable. That is the whole idea: structure, channel, link.
"I'd look at three levels. The structure: differential impedance on a TDR, typically 100 ohms, and the skew within the pair.
The channel: mixed-mode S-parameters on a VNA, so SDD21 for insertion loss, SDD11 for return loss, SCD21 for mode conversion, and crosstalk to neighbours.
And the link: an eye diagram with eye height, width, jitter and mask margin, or a BER. The eye is the result; the others tell me why."
Quick check. Which measurement tells you the differential impedance versus position along a pair?
